documentation.range: This species is distributed in the western Atlantic from Bermuda, the Flower Garden Banks in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico and Mexico (Veracruz) to south Florida and the Bahamas southward throughout the Caribbean to Trinidad and Tobago. The depth range is 1-43 metres but the species is most common shallower than 12 m (Goreau and Wells 1967).
documentation.population:
This species is common in most Greater Caribbean reef environments, but typically occurs in low abundances. 

Curaçao and Bonaire have some of the least degraded reefs in the Caribbean (Jackson et al. 2014). Off Curaçao, average island wide cover (in percentage of bottom cover) of this species decreased from 0.70 in 1973 (n=21 sites) to 0.10% (n=153 sites) in 2005 (Carmabi unpubl. data) based on direct observation. The abundance of this species is lower on neighbouring islands of Aruba (0.02%, n=52 sites,; Carmabi unpubl. data) and Bonaire (0.0% in 2014) (De Bakker et al. 2016) and there was a decline from an average cover of 0.02 in 1973 based on direct observation (De Bakker et al. 2016). This is a decrease of >56% in two localities with relatively healthy reefs (Bonaire and Curaçao).

This species can be abundant in some areas. It is thought to be more tolerant to high sedimentation and other stressors compared to other coral species (Hubbard and Pocock 1972, Pratte and Richardson 2014) and this may account for its ability to dominate certain human impacted areas (M. Vermeij and V. Chamberland pers. comm.) and naturally marginal coral reef systems (Dodge and Vaisnys 1977). Nonetheless, severe declines of this species have been reported in response to coastal development (Vermeij 2019) and construction activities (Dodge and Vaisnys 1977) as well as due to Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD; Meyer et al. 2019). with prevalence and losses of 67% in Grecian Rocks, Florida Keys (Lunz et al. 2017), 25% in Mexican Caribbean reefs (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019) and between 20-34% in the Bahamas (Dahlgren 2020).

Species-specific, global level population information is limited. However, coral reefs are experiencing severe global level declines due to increasing water temperatures caused by climate change (Hughes et al. 2018). For the purposes of this Red List assessment, we used species-specific vulnerability traits and two analytical approaches based on two global coral datasets to infer past (GCRMN 2021) and future (UNEP 2020) population trends.     

Approach 1: Future population trend

The projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) was applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. ASB represents the date at which a coral reef will likely experience severe bleaching conditions annually, and beyond which the species will experience a greater than 80% decline as it is not expected to recover (van Hooidonk et al. 2014). ASB is defined as at least eight Degree Heating Weeks (DHW) occurring over a three-month period within a year, and where a DHW occurs when the sea surface temperature is at least 1°C above the maximum monthly mean (van Hooidonk et al. 2014; 2015). We defined the onset of ASB as corresponding to 80% or more decline, however, this is conservative as other studies have found that corals are unlikely to recover with just two incidences of ASB per decade (Obura et al. 2022). 

To calculate ASB for each species we applied spatial data made publicly available via a United Nations Environment Programme report (UNEP 2020) that used the 2019 IPCC CMIP6 global climate models to estimate the projected onset of ASB for the years 2015-2100 on a 27 km x 27 km grid according to the 2018 WCMC-UNEP global coral reef distribution map, which has a resolution to 30 m depth. These data are available via two scenarios of Shared Socioeconomic Pathways (SSP), with SSP5-8.5 representing current global emissions and SSP2-4.5 representing a future reduction in emissions (UNEP 2020). We applied SSP5-8.5 since it follows the precautionary approach recommended by the IUCN Red List methodology and SSP2-4.5 since it represents a more moderate climate change scenario that better tracks current policy projections (Roelfsema et al. 2020, Obura et al. 2022). To acknowledge varying levels of coral adaptation to thermal stress, both of these spatial data layers are available for all quarter degree intervals between 0° and 2°C (UNEP 2020); however, coral adaptation in general is poorly understood and varies by species and locality (van Hooidonk et al. 2013, Logan et al. 2014). To account for adaptation, we calculated two estimates of ASB onset for both the SSP5-8.5 and the SSP2-4.5, where the first estimate assumes the species has no level of adaptation (0°C) and the second assumes a capacity for 1°C of adaptation. We clipped each of these four UNEP (2020) spatial data layers to the species’ distribution and calculated the average year of ASB onset across all overlapping grid cells.

Based on this spatial analysis, the onset of ASB across this species’ range is projected to occur on average by the year 2030 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2034 for SSP2-4.5 assuming no level of adaptation and by the year 2059 for SSP5-8.5 and by 2072 for SSP2-4.5 assuming 1°C of adaptation. We inferred that the uncertainty associated with the estimate of population decline based on no level of adaptation is lower given this species is primarily restricted to depths shallower than 30 m and is highly susceptible to bleaching. The relative vulnerability to bleaching (i.e., highly susceptible, moderately susceptible, or more resilient) is primarily based on scientific species expert knowledge. The application of the species’ depth range as a vulnerability factor is based on the understanding that a coral species with shallow depth preferences is more frequently exposed to extreme temperatures and is expected to decline at a faster global rate than species that also or primarily occur in deeper, cooler waters (Riegl and Piller 2003). Ocean acidification, which is measured by aragonite saturation, is also considered a major threat to corals due to the impacts of climate change, however, the impacts are expected to be more severe in cooler and/or deeper waters (Couce et al. 2013, van Hooidonk et al. 2014, Hoegh-Guldberg et al. 2017). Although the exact threshold of aragonite saturation that is expected to cause significant decline is not well-known, in the Atlantic, changes in aragonite saturation are expected to be most severe in the Mediterranean Sea (Flecha et al. 2015). Therefore, this species is inferred to experience a projected global level decline of at least 80% by the year 2050, or three generations in the future, regardless of the SSP2-4.5 or SSP5-8.5 scenario. 

Approach 2: Past population trend

Coral reef monitoring data was also applied as a proxy to estimate global level population decline. The Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network (GCRMN) compiled data related to the status and trends of coral reefs in 10 regions from 1978-2019 via the scientific monitoring observations of more than 300 network members located throughout the world. We applied the publicly available data on estimations of the percent of live hard coral cover loss at the 20%, 50% and 80% confidence intervals in the five Caribbean subregions (GCRMN 2021) to estimate species population decline over the past three generations (1989-2019). The proportion of the species’ range that overlapped with each of the subregions was estimated using the Red List distribution map. The sum of the proportion of the subregional species distribution multiplied by the percent of coral cover loss in each subregion was then used to calculate the 20%, 50% and 80% estimates of coral loss across this species’ entire range.

To inform the choice of the best (i.e., lowest level of uncertainty) out of the three percentile declines, we considered nine species-specific traits related to vulnerability to coral cover loss. Given this species’ depth range is 1-43 m and is predominately found at depths less than 10 m, generalized abundance is considered common, overall population is not highly fragmented, does not occur off-reef, is highly susceptible to disease, is highly susceptible to Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD), does recover well from bleaching or disease and is highly susceptible to bleaching, it is overall inferred to be highly susceptible to threats related to reef degradation. Therefore, past decline was inferred from the 80% percentile of estimated coral cover loss, resulting in a global level decline of 28% since 1989, or over the past three generations.
documentation.habitats:
This species occurs in lagoon and back- and fore-reef environments (Goreau and Wells 1967). This is a hermaphroditic protogynous spawner with an annual cycle of gametogenesis. The timing of gamete release differs among locations throughout the Caribbean. Spawning occurs between April and November, but most commonly between June and August (Szmant 1986, Soong 1991, Jordan 2018). On Curaçao and Bonaire, this species spawns between April and November with a peak in June (Chamberland et al. 2017, E. Muller pers. comm.). However, it reproduces during the late summer in Mexico (S. Snowden pers. obs.), while in Puerto Rico (Weil and Vargas 2010) and Colombia (Alvarado et al. 2004) it spawns only during a single spawning event in the spring. In Mexico, this species spawns in July and August (Grosso-Becerra et al. 2021). Spawning generally occurs between 8 to 13 days after the full moon, with a peak around 11 to 12 days after the full moon. Schools of butterflyfish swarming around a colony typically indicate imminent or ongoing spawning of this colony. Colonies often spawn in up to three consecutive pulses that last in average 5 min and are spaced by intervals of 3 to 20 minutes (Chamberland et al. 2017). This is the only Caribbean coral species that spawns prior to sunset (Muller and Vermeij 2011, Chamberland et al. 2017, Jordan 2018). It generally exhibits high rates of recruitment, but new recruits may sustain high mortality.

Populations comprise cryptic species, at least on Curaçao. Genetically isolated, but morphologically similar groupings of Diploria labyrinthiformis colonies exist that spawn during different periods of the year (spring vs. fall; V. Chamberland unpubl. data). Genome-wide sequencing confirms that colonies spawning in different seasons represented distinct genetic clusters (Fst= 0.126), showing that different spawning periods have resulted in (partial) reproductive isolation among sympatric, morphologically similar colonies (V. Chamberland unpubl. data). Effective populations size for this species that are already in decline (see above) are thus even smaller than those derived from species inventories based on morphology alone.

The age at first maturity of most reef-building corals is typically three to eight years (Wallace 1999). Based on this, we infer that the average age of mature individuals of this species is greater than eight years. Based on average sizes and growth rates, we also infer that the average length of one generation is 10 years. Longevity is not known, but is likely to be greater than 10 years. Therefore, any population decline rates estimated for the purposes of this Red List assessment are measured over a time period of 30 years.
documentation.threats:
This species is highly susceptible to a multitude of common Caribbean coral diseases (Garzón-Ferreira et al. 2001, Nugues 2002, Precht et al. 2016). It is highly susceptible to Stony Coral Tissue Loss Disease (SCTLD) and is highly sensitive and highly vulnerable to climate change (Foden et al. 2013). SCTLD was first described in Florida in 2014 (Precht et al. 2016) and subsequently spread among Caribbean reefs (https://www.agrra.org/coral-disease-outbreak/#sctld-dashboard). Prevalence of SCTLD among populations of this species has been reported at 67% in Grecian Rocks, Florida Keys (Lunz et al. 2017), up to 80% in Puerto Rico (Weil et al. 2019), between 20-34% in the Bahamas (Dahlgren 2020), and from 25-44% in the Mexican Caribbean (Alvarez-Filip et al. 2019, L. Alvarez-Filip pers. comm. 2020). Complete mortality of colonies commonly occurs within weeks to months. A recent study in which a small population was monitored in Jardines Reef, Mexican Caribbean showed that 7 out of 9 colonies died within months of being infected (Grosso-Becerra et al. 2021). This emerging disease represents a new and significant threat to the species' status. Other diseases that significantly threaten this species are Black Band and White Plague diseases (Gintert et al. 2019).

In general, the major threat to corals is global climate change, in particular, temperature extremes leading to bleaching and increased susceptibility to disease, increased severity of ENSO events and storms, and ocean acidification (Richards et al. 2008). The most recent, and first, multi-year, global bleaching event (spanning hundreds of kilometres or more) was from 2014 to 2017. Nearly 30% of reefs suffered mortality level-stress, more than 50% of affected reef areas were impacted at least twice, and some locations saw almost complete coral cover loss (Blunden et al. 2018, Vargas-Angel et al. 2019, Eakin et al. 2019). The average interval between bleaching events is now more than 50% less than before, preventing full reef recovery (Hughes et al. 2018).

Coral disease has emerged as a serious threat to coral reefs worldwide and is a major cause of reef deterioration (Weil et al. 2006, Richards et al. 2008, Maynard et al. 2015). As noted in Walton et al. (2018), in addition to thermal stress, increased coral disease prevalence and mortality can be linked to reduced water quality (Bruno et al. 2003) and clarity (van Woesik and McCaffrey 2017), nutrient enrichment (Vega Thurber et al. 2013), dredging associated sedimentation (Pollock et al. 2014, Miller et al. 2016), and plastic pollution. Based on a survey of 159 reefs in the Asia-Pacific region, the likelihood of disease increases 20-fold when corals are in contact with plastic (Lamb et al. 2018). Increased coral disease levels on the GBR were correlated with increased ocean temperatures (Boyett et al. 2007) supporting the prediction that disease levels will be increasing with higher sea surface temperatures.

Localized threats to corals include fisheries and overfishing, bioerosion by sponges and other organisms, hurricane damage, high sedimentation. human development (industry, settlement, resort development, tourism, and transportation), changes in native species dynamics (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), invasive species (competitors, predators, pathogens and parasites), dynamite fishing, chemical fishing, pollution from agriculture and industry, domestic pollution, sedimentation, marine debris and human recreation and tourism activities. The severity of these combined threats to the global population of each individual coral species is not known.
documentation.measures:
All corals are listed on CITES Appendix II. In U.S. waters, it is illegal to harvest corals for commercial purposes. In the U.S., this species is present in most marine protected areas (MPAs) throughout the Caribbean.

This is a hermaphroditic broadcast spawner with a convenient schedule including multiple, daytime spawning events over five or six months of the year in Curaçao (Chamberland et al. 2017). As a result of this and its relative ease of larval culture, it is becoming the target of increasing larval propagation and restoration efforts (see http://crc.reefresilience.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/CSFS-Diploria-labyrinthiformis_June_2020.pdf).

Recommended measures for conserving this species include research and implementation of mitigation of SCTLD, likely including cryopreservation of genetic material that can be used in future restoration actions (Grosso-Becerra et al. 2021). Coral biorepositories that include cryopreserved Diploria labyrinthiformis sperm have been established in Mexico (Coralium-UNAM) and Curaçao (Carmabi). Other needs include species specific population abundance trends, taxonomy, ecology and habitat status, threats and resilience to threats, restoration action; identification, establishment and management of new protected areas; expansion of protected areas; recovery management; and disease, pathogen and parasite management.
documentation.rationale: This widely distributed coral species is common. Global level, species-specific population data are limited; however, coral reefs have declined globally and are expected to continue rapidly declining due to increasing severe bleaching conditions under temperature stress caused by climate change as well as a variety of other threats. Our species-specific vulnerability traits analysis indicates this species is highly susceptible to major threats related to coral reef degradation (e.g., disease and bleaching). We applied two analytical approaches involving two different global coral datasets and the species’ distribution map as proxies to infer population decline. Based on global coral cover monitoring data, this species experienced an inferred decline of about 28% over the past three generations, or since 1989. Based on the projected onset of annual severe bleaching (ASB) conditions via both SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios of global climate model data, in combination with the species’ depth range and bleaching vulnerability, this species is inferred to decline by at least 80% over the next three generations, or by 2050. Since the species qualifies for a higher category under the projected decline, we therefore list it as Critically Endangered A3c. The change in status from the previous assessment reflects updated declines calculated from improved data on modelled coral cover loss in the Caribbean from 1978 to 2019 and projected date of annual severe bleaching, along with improved knowledge of species traits.
